opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think GPUs are going to continue to play a very important role. They're incredibly versatile machines, and that versatility is exactly why they won training. When you're training a model, you need a general-purpose, highly programmable engine that can handle whatever the researchers throw at it, and NVIDIA has built a phenomenal ecosystem around that.

But inference is a different animal. Once a model is trained and you deploy it, the problem shifts. Now you care about cost per token, latency, energy efficiency, and how many users you can serve on a given amount of power and real estate in the data center. And inference isn't one monolithic market. You have applications that need very low latency, like interactive agents, coding assistants, or real-time voice, where the user is waiting on every token. Then you have batch workloads where throughput matters more than responsiveness. You have small models running at the edge, and you have very large models with long context windows running in the cloud. Those are very different requirements.

So my view is that the inference market is going to be heterogeneous. GPUs will serve a chunk of it, especially where flexibility matters or where people already have the infrastructure in place. But for a lot of these workloads, a GPU is overkill in some dimensions and underpowered in others. The biggest bottleneck in generative inference today is memory bandwidth, not raw compute. You're constantly moving weights and KV cache in and out of memory, and the GPU architecture, with HBM sitting off to the side, wasn't designed with that as the primary constraint.

That's really why we started d-Matrix. We said, if inference is going to be the dominant workload over time, and we believe it will be, then you need purpose-built silicon that brings compute and memory much closer together, so you can deliver fast, interactive inference at much better efficiency. I don't see it as GPUs versus everyone else. I see a world where customers pick the right tool for each application, and the economics of inference will force that. When you're serving billions of queries a day, a few-x improvement in cost and energy is not a nice-to-have. It decides whether a business model works at all.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference as heterogeneous and says customers will choose the right tool for each application, implying no single chip serves every need.

r002.rationale: It calls GPUs overkill in some dimensions and notes their architecture was not designed around memory bandwidth, but does not clearly identify their general-purpose design as the source of inference inefficiency.

r003.rationale: The response names differing needs such as latency and throughput, but does not clearly state that GPUs are poorly suited to applications requiring a particular performance metric to be fully optimized.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Look, I think GPUs have earned their place. They were the right tool for the training era, and frankly they're still the right tool for a lot of workloads where you need maximum flexibility and you're not constrained by power or cost. I don't think anyone should be predicting the death of the GPU.

But inference is a different animal. When you train a model, you do it once, in a data center, with essentially unlimited power and a budget that matches. When you deploy that model, you're running it millions or billions of times, and you're running it in places that look nothing like a data center. A camera on a factory floor. A robot. A car. A piece of medical equipment. A retail edge box sitting in a closet somewhere. Each of those has a completely different set of constraints around latency, power, cost, and form factor.

And that's where the general-purpose approach starts to break down. A GPU was fundamentally designed to be a very good parallel processor for graphics, and then it was repurposed for AI. It carries a lot of silicon and a lot of software overhead that you don't need if all you want to do is run a known set of models as efficiently as possible. So you end up paying for flexibility you're not using, in watts and in dollars.

The way I think about it, the inference market is going to fragment. You'll have the big cloud players continuing to use GPUs and their own custom silicon for the heaviest workloads. And then you'll have this enormous long tail of edge applications where what wins is performance per watt and performance per dollar on the actual models people are deploying, not peak TOPS on a spec sheet. That's where purpose-built inference architectures make sense, and that's the bet we've made at d-Matrix.

The other piece that people underestimate is memory. For a lot of inference workloads, especially with transformers and large language models, you're not compute-bound, you're memory-bound. You're moving data back and forth between memory and compute, and that's where the power goes. That's why we've focused on in-memory compute, bringing the computation to where the data lives, rather than just stacking more cores. A GPU can throw more bandwidth at that problem, but it's an expensive way to solve it.

So to answer your question directly: GPUs will remain a big part of the inference market, but their share will shrink as the market matures and as customers get more sophisticated about what they actually need. Five years from now I think we'll look back and see that the one-size-fits-all era was really just the first chapter.

r001.rationale: It says inference needs will fragment across workloads and markets, with cloud GPUs and custom silicon alongside purpose-built chips for edge applications, and calls the one-size-fits-all era an early chapter.

r002.rationale: It describes GPUs as carrying silicon and software overhead that inference may not need, making customers pay in watts and dollars for unused flexibility.

r003.rationale: It says edge workloads favor performance per watt and per dollar, while GPU flexibility and overhead make GPUs a costly fit for those applications.

astra-6.text:
I think GPUs will continue to play a very important role, but inference is not a one-size-fits-all market. Different applications have different requirements. If you’re serving an interactive application, latency matters a lot. If you’re processing a large batch of requests in the background, you may care more about throughput and cost. At the edge, power consumption can be the biggest constraint.

GPUs offer tremendous flexibility, and that’s valuable when models and workloads are changing quickly. But that doesn’t mean they’ll be the optimal solution for every application. There’s room for specialized hardware that delivers better efficiency for particular inference needs. I see a heterogeneous market, where the application’s requirements determine which compute platform makes the most sense.

r001.rationale: The response says inference is “not a one-size-fits-all market” and that application requirements determine which compute platform makes sense.

r002.rationale: It notes GPU flexibility and says GPUs may not be optimal for every application, but does not identify their general-purpose design as a source of inference inefficiency.

r003.rationale: It names latency, throughput, cost, and power as application needs, but does not clearly state that GPUs are poorly suited when a particular performance metric must be fully optimized.

sol-6.1.text:
I think GPUs will continue to play a very important role, but inference is a diverse market. You have applications where you need a response almost instantaneously, and others where you can batch requests and optimize for throughput. Those are different requirements.

So I don’t see this as one architecture winning everything. GPUs offer flexibility, and that’s valuable when models and workloads are changing quickly. But as applications mature, there’s an opportunity for specialized hardware that delivers better efficiency for a particular workload. The question becomes: what latency, throughput, power consumption, and cost does that application need? That’s what will determine the right platform.

r001.rationale: It says no single architecture will win everything and describes inference needs as varying by application, which communicates that one chip cannot serve them all.

r002.rationale: It says GPUs are flexible and specialized hardware may be more efficient for particular workloads, but does not identify GPUs’ general-purpose design as the source of inference inefficiency.

r003.rationale: It lists differing latency and throughput needs, but does not say GPUs are poorly suited to applications that require a particular metric to be fully optimized.
